stem: In which year did the **Economic Structural Adjustment Programme (ESAP)** begin?

stem: State **four** challenges faced by Zimbabwe since independence.

points.description: Drought / cyclones and floods
Economic difficulties (ESAP, hyperinflation, unemployment, currency changes)
Disease (HIV and AIDS, cholera, COVID-19)
Brain drain / sanctions or restrictive measures / the disturbances of the 1980s

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Drought, hyperinflation, HIV and AIDS, and brain drain.

stem: Explain **two** effects of the severe drought of the early 1990s on Zimbabwe.

points.description: Crop failure
Developed: maize had to be imported and many families depended on food aid
Death of livestock / water shortages
Developed: farmers lost cattle (wealth and draught power); towns rationed water

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Crops failed across the country, so maize had to be imported and many families depended on food aid. Many cattle died, so farmers lost wealth and draught power, and towns faced water shortages.

hints: Think of food, livestock and water.

stem: Suggest **three** ways in which Zimbabwe could reduce the brain drain, explaining how each would help.

points.description: Better pay and conditions
Developed: removes the main reason skilled workers leave
Housing, transport or loan schemes / career development
Developed: makes staying more attractive than leaving
Encourage the diaspora to return or invest / economic stability
Developed: skills and money come back; stable prices make salaries worth more

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The government and employers could improve pay and working conditions, removing the main reason why nurses and teachers leave. They could offer housing or vehicle loan schemes and chances for further training, making it more attractive to stay. They could also encourage people in the diaspora to return or invest, and keep prices stable so that local salaries keep their value.

stem:
**Source A** — a report in a fictional community newsletter in Chipinge, 2026 (invented for this question)

> Seven years after Cyclone Idai, the rebuilt bridge on our road is finally open. Families who lost their homes in 2019 now live in new houses on higher ground. Many still remember the night the river rose and the hills slid down. The council has planted trees on the slopes and set up an early-warning committee in every ward.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which type of challenge does Source A describe?

options.rationale: Correct: a cyclone with floods and landslides.

parts.explanation: Cyclone Idai was a natural disaster.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: According to Source A, families were resettled on higher ground.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Using the source, explain **two** measures that could reduce the effects of a future cyclone.

points.description: Planting trees on slopes
Developed: roots hold the soil, reducing landslides
Early-warning committees / building on higher ground

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Planting trees on the slopes helps, because roots hold the soil and reduce landslides. Early-warning committees in every ward can warn people to move to safety in time, and building on higher ground keeps homes out of the floodwater.

stem: Answer the questions on the economic challenges since 1990.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the main features of ESAP.

points.description: Began in 1991 with support from international lenders
Cut government spending / civil service jobs
Removed price controls
Opened the economy to imports / introduced fees for some services

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: ESAP began in 1991 with loans from international lenders. The government cut its spending and civil service jobs, removed price controls, opened the economy to imports and introduced fees for some school and health services.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: "Sanctions were the main cause of Zimbabwe's economic difficulties in the 2000s." Discuss.

points.description: View that they were the main cause: the government and its supporters argue that cut credit, investment and trade damaged the whole economy; SADC and the AU called for removal
Opposing view: Western governments say the measures were targeted at individuals and companies; humanitarian aid continued
Other causes: falling farm output, economic policy, debt, corruption, drought
Supported judgement

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant points or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge and examples, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The government and its supporters argue that sanctions were the main cause. They say that the measures cut Zimbabwe off from international credit and investment and discouraged trade, damaging the whole economy, and SADC and the African Union have called for their removal.

Western governments disagree. They describe the measures as targeted restrictive measures on named individuals and companies, and point out that humanitarian aid continued.

Many observers argue that several causes worked together: falling farm output in the early 2000s, economic policy decisions, debt, corruption and drought.

In my judgement the measures played a part, especially by limiting credit, but they were one cause among several rather than the only or main one.

explanation: Describing ESAP and discussing a contested issue.
hints: Present each view fairly before your judgement.
